derivation.method: lab/verify-ground-truth.py, run from inside labnet via `lab/run.sh verify`. Python standard-library sockets only: it shares no code, no port table and no fingerprint data with bathy, and it consults neither Nmap nor any of its data files. Every `product`/`version` below is transcribed from a banner that script read -- verbatim, which `xtask check-lab` now enforces by requiring each one to appear in its own `evidence` string, or else to declare `product_inference` saying what non-literal basis it rests on. `lab/README.md` quotes the banners in full.
derivation.swept_ports: 1-65535 TCP on every address listed here, including the absent ones
derivation.known_to_be_wrong_before: Until the M7 Task 1 fix round, 10.30.0.17:443 recorded `product: null` while the response it was transcribed from carries `Server: nginx/1.29.8`. AC-7.5's test skips endpoints whose product is null, so the null exempted the one endpoint where bathy also reports nothing -- the oracle recorded what the scanner found rather than what is there. The entry now states the product; see its `identification_gap`.

open.evidence: accepts a connection and volunteers no bytes; PostgreSQL speaks only when spoken to, so the lab establishes that something is listening here and does not establish a product name

open.product_inference: The bytes name the version (9.4.0) and the default authentication plugin (caching_sha2_password) but never the string `MySQL`. The product name is read off the wire format -- a protocol-10 handshake whose default plugin is caching_sha2_password -- not transcribed from a literal, which is why this is the one entry that cannot satisfy check-lab's product-appears-in-evidence rule and says so instead of being exempted silently. MariaDB, the other protocol-10 speaker, prefixes its version with `5.5.5-` and defaults to mysql_native_password.

open.evidence: \x05\x00\x00\x00\x0b\x08\x05\x1a\x00 -- the X Protocol port the mysql image also opens. Recorded because it is open, not because bathy identifies it: an oracle that omitted it would turn a correct finding into a false positive.

a plaintext GET on this port returns `HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request\r\nServer: nginx/1.29.8\r\n ... <hr><center>nginx/1.29.8</center>`. The 400 establishes a TLS listener; the `Server` header names the product and version outright, in cleartext, before any TLS handshake.
open.identification_gap: bathy reports no product here, and this entry records what is on the wire rather than what bathy finds. The cause is not a missing rule: `http.server.nginx.v1` matches these exact bytes (see `the_bytes_a_tls_terminator_returns_to_a_plaintext_request_name_its_product` in crates/bathy-interpret/src/rules.rs). It is Scheduler::detect_service's policy of stopping at the first probe whose capture interprets to anything -- on 443 that is `tls-v1`, which is protocol-only by construction because RFC 8446 encrypts the certificate, so `http-get-v1` never runs. Changing that policy changes per-endpoint packet accounting (AC-4.24), pacing (AC-4.26) and the reported `service` for every TLS port, so it is a scanner change and not a fix-round change. AC-7.5's test holds this endpoint to being UNidentified: the day bathy names it, that test fails and demands this key be deleted.
